newsitem.title: CANADA: New refugee move lessens military need - Canada.
newsitem.headline: New refugee move lessens military need - Canada.

text.p: Hundreds of thousands of refugees appeared to be heading through eastern Zaire toward the Rwandan border in a new mass exodus, Canadian Defence Minister Doug Young said on Wednesday.

"Information we have seems to indicate strongly enough that hundreds of thousands more that might still be in the region are on their way from the southern part of the eastern region of Zaire towards Bukavu to return to Rwanda," he said.

Previous reports spoke of tens of thousands, perhaps as many as 100,000, on the move. Relief officials say that over the past week about half a million left the Goma region of eastern Zaire for northern Rwanda but hundreds of thousands remained in the Bukavu region opposite southern Rwanda.

The U.N. Security Council on Friday mandated a Canadian-led force to open up corridors to help refugees return home and to get aid both to refugees and to Zaireans who have been displaced within their own country.

But the need for that force -- to have been led by Canada and including the United States, Britain, France, Spain and others -- was being re-examined in meetings in New York on Wednesday and in Stuttgart, Germany, on Friday.

"The more refugees coming into Rwanda of course the less need for a strong military intervention," U.N. envoy Raymond Chretien said from the Zairean capital Kinshasa in an interview with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.

But he cautioned against thinking only about Rwandan refugees. He spoke of about 100,000 refugees in Zaire from neighbouring Burundi and "a few hundred thousand Zairois (Zairians). We should not forget about the displaced Zairois."
In any case, even if there would still be a military force, the attention has shifted much more to providing aid.

"There is no question that the humanitarian aspect is taking on more and more importance as the situation on the ground seems to be sorting itself out with respect to refugees being able to return home," Young told reporters. "The situation has changed so dramatically that the military mission certainly would now seem to be a lot less of a focus than it was 10 days ago."

Chretien, a nephew of Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien, who has led the drive to get help to Zaire, said armed Hutu groups that had been among the refugees in camps near Goma had retreated into the Zairian forests.
"They obviously will have to be dealt with later on. But this military danger is no longer there," he said. He said it seemed there were "very, very few refugees" left with those Hutu militias.

Canadian politicians and media have been generally supportive of Ottawa's lead in the crisis and about 25 Zairians demonstrated in front of the Canadian Parliament on Wednesday in support of Canada's action.
But some newspaper commentators have questioned the prime minister's motives in the affair.

"When it looked like the world was going to leave nephew Ray, and by extension Canada, twisting in the wind, it became a matter of pride and face," wrote the Sun newspapers' Sean Durkan. "Chretien's intervention was born of cool, self-serving pragmatism."

Southam News columnist Giles Gherson wrote on Sunday: "For years, Canadian prime ministers eager to make their mark on the international stage have been tempted to beg their advisers: 'Find me a Suez crisis' -- the 1956 Middle East dust-up calmed by Canadian-led diplomacy. Chretien just landed himself one."
